start.text: The chapter will sit. I've said so, and I'll say it again until the candles let it.
Still choosing for yourself, Wakebearer? I've not stopped hoping you'll tire of it.
Wakebearer. Have you thought on the rite?
The crown, Wakebearer. They'll not leave the wall till they see you up there.
The door's open, and the cradle's at the top. I've nothing to add to what the chapter said.

first.text: A tall woman in a white robe stands at the top of the chapter-house steps, a red stole over her shoulders and her hands folded at her waist, as if she has stood exactly there since the bell.
Wakebearer. Forgive me not coming down to the quay. Nobody on Kindleby goes further from the candles than they must. Not even me.
Agathe Lorn. Provost of Kindleby. These days that means I'm the most senior Keeper anyone can find.
Have we met? ...No. I'd remember an ember.
Four lights. The Gull, the Ridge, the Heron, the Wrack. We've had the news of every one off the Tidewright decks, a week late and wrong in the particulars. You'll tell me the particulars, one day.
You carry a sleeve-ember. That's off a Spire robe, and it's been picked off with a thumbnail. ...Aldous Wren. He always did pick at things.
He ran home to Saltmarrow, then. They all ran, that night. Aldous ran the furthest, and the least far.
There's a story going round the Tidewright decks that Keepers put the Spire out. On purpose. It started on Wrackholm, they say, from a stranger with an ember.
I'd like it to stop. Stories like that get people drowned.
And sworn a friend of the lanes, I hear. Their oath is about decks. Ours is about light. A person can carry both, if they're careful which one they set down first.

choice.text: What would it take to light the Vigil Light?
About the rite...
Aldous told me the High Keeper put the flame out.
Wynn Sallow is alive. He keeps the Ridge Light on Thornwold.
There's a Keeper at the Ridge Light on Thornwold. He calls himself the Lamp.
There are colliers on the Northing's boat-stage, waiting for the Spire's boat. I promised I'd tell the Spire.
Aldous Wren wrote to you.
This came out of the Vigil Light's smoke, into my hand.
Sister Hild would row me out to the Low Water, with your leave.
Who's in the Quiet House?
My ember could hold the ring while the chapter sits.
What else did the chapter weigh?
Brother Iver's home.
Brother Iver's alive. He's keeping Lowsong's light, and he's staying.
Goodbye.

rite.text: Her hand goes to the long iron key on the chain at her belt, and rests there.
The Vigil Light, on the crown of the island above us. Dark, like the rest were. I have the key.
It will be lit, Wakebearer, and you will light it, and I thank the flame for you every night. But not the way the others were.
On four islands now you chose what was burned. You. Alone. A stranger with an ember, at the top of a stair, with whoever happened to be standing near.

That was never how it was done. For nine hundred years a Keeper chose. The chapter sat, and weighed, and chose what an island could spare, and the island never had to. That's what a Keeper is: one who chooses, so that others needn't.
So I'll ask you plainly. Bow to the rite. Let the chapter sit and choose Kindleby's burning, and carry its choice up the stair. That's all.

choice.text: I'll bow to the rite.
I'll choose, as I've chosen everywhere.
And if the chapter chooses wrong?
I'll think on it.

wrong.text: Then it will be the chapter's wrong, and not yours. Is that so small a thing to be given?

bowed.text: For a moment she looks very much older, and then she doesn't.
You don't know what it is to us, to have the thing done properly. Once. Since.
The chapter will sit. Not tonight; there are brothers and sisters on the candles, and the candles come first. But it will sit.

refused.text: Then the chapter will sit anyway, and choose anyway, and you'll do as you please at the top of the stair.
We'll see which of us Kindleby thanks. I don't think it'll be either.

aldous.text: Aldous Wren was a door-warden on the east stair, and he was drinking before he was a novice. He told you the High Keeper put out the Firstflame.
The order's word is that the Firstflame failed. The High Keeper was at the flame when it failed, and has not been seen since. That is what the order knows.
He saw a light go down the stair past him, that night.
She is quiet long enough for a candle on the sill behind her to gutter and recover.
If Aldous Wren has seen something, he can come to Kindleby and say it to the chapter. I'd send a boat for him. Tell him so.

lamp_told.text: She says it like a word in a language she used to speak.
Every beacon-keeper who'd sent no word by spring we wrote into the Long Book among the lost. Wynn Sallow of the Ridge Light among them. Thirty years on that ridge, and I wrote him off in a line.
I'll have the line struck through. We don't scrape a name out of the Long Book. We strike it, so anybody can see it was once wrong.

lamp_left.text: The Lamp. That's not a name, Wakebearer, that's a post. Every beacon-keeper is the Lamp to somebody.
The Ridge Light's keeper is in the Long Book. If he's chosen to go by no name, he'll have had his reasons. It's his to choose.

stage.text: The Northing's stage. Keepers' boats put in there once a month with oil and meal, for longer than anybody's counted.
And they've waited on it three months. For a boat from the Spire.
There is no Spire to tell, Wakebearer. There's me.
Very well. You've told the Spire. When the chapter sits I'll put it to them that the skiff goes north, with oil and meal and a lantern, and brings back whoever wants bringing.

quiet.text: Those the fog had. Brothers and sisters off the Spire who came over in the boats Hushed, and anybody the boats have found drifting since.
Those the fog had. Brothers and sisters off the Spire, and anybody found drifting. How the old ones came to us, I couldn't tell you. We've always kept the Hushed.
We keep them warm, and fed, and near the candles. It's the oldest work of the order, Wakebearer. Older than the beacons. To keep the Hushed.
You can't go in. Not with that in your hand. They've had enough of other people's light.

offer.text: She looks past you, down the steps and along the wall, to a sister bent over her candles with her hood up.
Every one of them on the wall since the Snuffing, turn and turn. Some of the old ones haven't sat down an hour together in three months.
An hour is all the chapter needs, if it's let.
You refused the rite, and you'll keep the door for it to sit. I don't understand you, Wakebearer. Thank you.
Go up to the crown and stand by the Vigil Light, where every candle on the ring can see you. When they see you there, we'll let them gutter.

weighed.text: We weighed the Long Book, and wouldn't. A name in it is all some of them have left.
We weighed the candles. If Kindleby forgot the vigil we'd stop lighting them, and the fog would be at the door by morning.
And we weighed the night the boats came. The old ones don't sleep, Wakebearer. Brother Anselm sits up on the wall till dawn and calls it his turn. Kindleby can spare a night.

choice.text: It's the only night anybody here saw what happened at the Spire.
Then I'll think on it.

weighed_spire.text: Her hand is on the key at her belt again.
I never asked them, Wakebearer. I told you that. Carry it up, or don't. It's been chosen.

after.text: She touches the key at her belt, and seems to remember it is only a key now.
You chose as the chapter chose. I'll not ask whether you meant to.
You bowed to the rite, Wakebearer. On those steps. And then you went up the stair and did as you pleased.
The chapter will write it down: that the rite was kept, and broken, the same night. We write everything down.
You said you'd choose, and you chose. Brother Tobin came to me after and asked why he'd been crying. I couldn't tell him.
Brother Anselm keeps going down to the quay of an evening and looking at the water. I've told him there's nothing coming.
The old ones still don't sleep. I'd thought, by now, one of them might tell me why.
The skiff's gone north, as I said it would. Two of my sisters, with oil and meal and a lantern. If the Northing's stage still has anybody on it, they'll bring them.
The skiff came back light. Sister Hild says your colliers took the meal and went home up the steps. Good. I'd have kept them, gladly.
Your colliers are on my wall. They keep candles better than half my sisters; Wenna Coll says a candle's only a clamp turned inside out. I've given them the chapter-house fire. We'll keep them.
The skiff came back with nobody in it. Sister Hild says the stage was empty and the fire raked out. She left the meal anyway. She always did.
Five lights, Wakebearer. The Spire next, I suppose, and the chapter can't sit for that one. There's nobody there to hold the door.

letter.text: You give it into her hand. She looks at the outside a long moment, then unfolds it and reads it standing at the door, all the way through, and then again from the top. A candle on the sill behind her gutters and recovers, twice.
He spelled my name wrong. He always did.
He says a light went down the east stair past him, the night the Spire went dark. Going down. Not going out.
He says he'll come when the Spire's lit, or when it isn't worth lighting, whichever's first. A door-warden's answer. He always had one.
She folds it along his folds and puts it in her sleeve.
There's a page at the back of the Long Book for what was seen. Not who was lost: what was seen. It's empty. It's been empty a long while. I never asked why.
I'll put him on it. In my own hand. The chapter can read it when it next sits, and do as it likes.

taper.text: She doesn't take it. She looks at it in your hand, and runs her eye down the notches the way you'd count stairs.

A stair-taper. The east stair at the Spire is two hundred and some steps in the dark, with the wind coming down it off the lantern room. A novice is given one of these at the foot, lit, to hold for the keepers going down. A notch for every landing, so they'll know where they are when it blows out.
Brother Aldous cut them. It was the one thing he did sober, all his life, and he did it well.
I said I'd remember an ember. I'd not remember a novice. There were a great many novices, and they all had the same face under the hood: frightened, and trying not to be.
She looks at your face as if trying it under a hood.
A light went down the east stair, he wrote. Going down. Not going out.
She doesn't finish. A candle on the sill behind her leans, and straightens.
Keep it out of the chapter's sight, Wakebearer. Out of mine, now I've seen it. They'd want to weigh it.

low_water.text: She is quiet long enough for a candle on the wall to gutter and be lit again.
Nobody goes out in the wet, Wakebearer. I said it the night of the Snuffing, and I've said it every morning since, and I've meant it every time.
I said it, and then I sent Hild north anyway, because you asked. I begin to think I only keep the rule so I've something to break for you.

Lowsong is Brother Iver Lusk's. Thirty-one winters alone on that rock. He'd row in at midsummer for his oil and argue the whole chapter round about the Long Book's commas, and row out again before Compline so nobody could answer him.
I wrote him in the Long Book three months ago, under the Snuffing, with the rest we've had no word of. I wrote him the way we write the drowned. Nobody went to see. I didn't send anybody to see.
It's a Keepers' light. And it's you asking.
Yes. Go. Tell Hild she's to bring you both back, and she's not to stop and listen.

iver_home.text: I know. He came up the steps behind Hild and asked me where his cell was. Thirty-one years, and he asked me.
I've struck him out of the Long Book. It's the first line I've ever struck. I did it with him stood there, and I'd do it again.
He doesn't know what he sat out there listening for. Hild won't say, and I've not asked her. Whatever the Low Water burned, it was his to give. I'll not weigh it.

iver_stays.text: Alive. ...And he'll not come in? Not even at midsummer, for the oil?
You tell her what burned. She listens to all of it, and when you've done she nods once, the way she'd take a report.
Then he doesn't know us. Well. He'll not come in to argue the commas, and I'll not have to lose.
I'll write him in again, under the light, where the living go. He'll not know. I will.

claim.text: The Provost stands at the head of the Boat Stair with her hands folded, the way she stood at the foot of the chapter-house steps, as if she's stood there since the boat came in.
For nine hundred years a Keeper chose what a beacon burned. Six times now you've chosen alone, at the top of a stair, and six times the islands let you, because there was nobody else to.
There's a chapter now. Not the whole of it: what I could put in a boat. It will go up to the Spire's foot and sit, and weigh what the Hearthspire can be given, and choose.
And you'll carry what it chooses up the stair. That's what you are to us, Wakebearer. The hand. Not the choosing.
You refused me once. I'm not asking this time.
You held Kindleby's door for an hour so the chapter could sit. Hold this one.

choice.text: The chapter can sit. I'll hear what it says.
I've chosen six times. I'll choose the seventh.

claim_refused.text: Then the chapter will sit anyway, and write down that you wouldn't listen. We write everything down.
She says it without heat, the way you'd say the tide will turn.

choice.text: Why come now? You said nobody goes out in the wet.
Let her hold the Stair-Taper and the Hood-Pin.
Tell her about the novices' roll.
The road up forgets where it goes. You'll want the cressets.
When does the chapter go up?
Leave her to the quay.

why.text: Because the Mercy went down the lane in, and Tobin's bell rang the once, and I found I couldn't stand on the quay steps and wait for the second.
And because six lights stand round this island now, and there was nobody at the middle but you. That was never how it was done.

weigh.text: I told you once to keep the taper out of the chapter's sight. Well. The chapter's come to it.
Let me hold them. That's all weighing is, to begin with. You hold a thing in your hands, and you ask what an island could spare.

choice.text: Put the Stair-Taper and the Hood-Pin in her hands.
No. They're mine.

weigh_shown.text: She holds the taper in one palm and the pin in the other, and her hands go still, the way hands go still on a bird.
Cold. A candle-end and a bit of bone. That's all they are, to me.
The ember stirs in your hand while she has them, and settles when she gives them back. She doesn't hurry.
The chapter will sit on them at the Spire's foot. Weighing isn't taking.

weigh_kept.text: Everything on the islands is somebody's, Wakebearer. That never once stopped the chapter.
Then it'll weigh you instead. It comes to the same thing, in the end.

roll.text: Aldous's roll. He kept it on a peg by his seat, and he'd let you read it if you brought him something for the cold.
You tell her: six names for the last midwinter in Aldous's hand, and a seventh place.

choice.text: Scraped. Down to the skin, with a blade.

roll_scraped.text: She's quiet long enough that Merrit starts humming again behind you.
Nobody scrapes a name. It's the first thing a novice is taught, before the candles: the Long Book doesn't forget, it only finishes. You strike it through, once, so anybody can see it was once wrong.
A Keeper's hand won't do the other thing. I've seen novices weep, trying to scrape a blot.

choice.text: Then it wasn't a Keeper.
Who kept the roll?

roll_not_keeper.text: Nobody but Keepers goes up to the crown. Nobody but Keepers could reach the peg.

roll_who.text: The door-warden. Aldous. And by the end he couldn't hold a pen straight, let alone a blade to vellum.
She doesn't say who else could have. She looks up the road, and doesn't say it.

roll_see.text: I'll want to see it. When the chapter goes up.

road.text: Hild says the road stops being a road a few yards up. Merrit says there are cressets.

road_lit.text: Seven lit, he says. He's told us three times since we tied up. You've lit the road for us, then.
Thank you. I mean it. You may not like what comes up it.

road_doused.text: Six, he says. And the road goes on past them.

choice.text: One was put out on purpose. The Unmoored sit under it. Leave it out.
Say nothing.

spare.text: ...A Keeper doesn't leave a light out because somebody in the dark asked her to, Wakebearer. That's all we are. The ones who don't.

relight.text: Hild takes the bow lantern off its crook and goes up the cinder road with it on a boat-hook. From the quay you watch the cressets you lit stand one above another up the moor in the fog, small and steady, and after a long while, above the last of them, another comes up.
Seven. Seven up the moor. Seven lit.
Hild comes back down an hour later with her hands black to the wrist.
Somebody'd packed that one with wet cinder and put a stone on it. Three days' work, that. I had it out in ten minutes.
There was a woman just past the light with a rake. She never said a word. When it caught she went off along the shoulder into the fog, and the rest of them after her.
Ness. She walked you up in the dark so it could stay out. It wasn't your fire. You don't think that will matter to her.
You asked. I heard you. It's written down.

stair_bye.text: We'll go up when I say. Not before. The chapter's tired, and it's a long way to carry a Long Book.

when.text: At dusk. The Long Book was always read by candle, and I'll not have it read any other way its first night at the Spire.
And not without you. A sitting with no hand to carry what it chooses is only a meeting.
And not without you, whatever you said. The chapter will want to see the hand it's writing down.

It takes them the rest of the day to make ready. Hild wraps the Long Book in its oilcloth and ties it on her back like a creel. By the time they go, the grey over the Boat Stair has gone the colour of a bruise, and the seven cressets stand up the moor one above another, the only warm things on Cindermoor.
Wenna Coll goes after the Keepers with her box of candles on her hip.
Iver goes last of the Keepers, stopping every few steps on the road with his head on one side.
Gone up. All of them. Up's all right, novice. It's the coming down I count.
The Provost goes up first, behind the cressets, and doesn't look back at the boat. They'll be at the Spire's foot before you.

foot.text: The Provost stands in the ring of candles with her hands folded, facing the niche: the lifted seat, and the dark under it.
Tomorrow. The candles first, and then the oldest book in the order. I've waited nine hundred years without knowing I was waiting. I can wait a night.
What you told me on the quay, about the roll. I've seen it now.
That's all she says about it.

lower.text: The Provost sits on the floor of the lower rooms with her back to the lectern's foot and the Spire's book over her head, reading the Long Book in her lap by candlelight. She doesn't get up.
Oriel wrote to me every midsummer for forty years. About the oil. About novices, and who'd make a door-warden. Never once about this. She sat on it as long as Aldous sat on the seat.
It's written now. In my hand. I'd sooner it were anybody's.
You wrote it like one of us. I watched you. You didn't have to think about the letters.
Open. I keep looking at the place. Nine hundred years and that's the only page in the Long Book anybody's ever left open.
The chapter will sit again before it chooses. Not tonight either. I want to know what we'd be choosing with.
